geelong.intro: Victoria’s second-largest city wraps around Corio Bay, an hour down the highway from Melbourne. The waterfront is the place to start: a long, walkable foreshore with the painted Baywalk Bollards, swimming enclosures and bay views. It’s also the gateway to the Bellarine Peninsula and the start of the Great Ocean Road country, so it works as a base or a first stop.

ballarat.intro: Ballarat grew rich in the 1850s gold rush, and it shows: grand Victorian streetscapes along Lydiard and Sturt streets, ornate arcades and old hotels. Sovereign Hill, the outdoor museum recreating a gold-rush town, is the big drawcard, and Lake Wendouree with its botanical gardens is made for an easy afternoon.

bendigo.intro: Another gold-rush city, Bendigo pairs grand 19th-century architecture with a serious arts scene. The Bendigo Art Gallery punches well above its weight with touring exhibitions, the Golden Dragon Museum tells the story of the city’s Chinese community, and you can head underground at the Central Deborah Gold Mine.

daylesford.intro: Daylesford and neighbouring Hepburn Springs sit in Victoria’s spa country, on the largest concentration of mineral springs in Australia. Come for the bathhouses and a slow weekend: Lake Daylesford, Wombat Hill Botanic Gardens, galleries, produce stores and long lunches in the surrounding hills.

bright.intro: Bright sits in the Ovens Valley at the foot of Mount Buffalo, the classic High Country base. Autumn turns the town’s European trees gold and red, the Murray to Mountains Rail Trail runs right through it, and the alpine resorts at Falls Creek and Mount Hotham are within a short drive in winter.

phillip-island.intro: Phillip Island is famous for the Penguin Parade at dusk, when little penguins come ashore at Summerland Beach. There’s plenty more: surf beaches, the Nobbies boardwalk and its seal colony views, koalas, and the Grand Prix motorcycle circuit. Cowes is the main town, with the cafés and most of the places to stay.

warrnambool.intro: Warrnambool sits at the western end of the Great Ocean Road. From roughly May to September, southern right whales come close to shore to calve, often visible from the viewing platform at Logans Beach. Flagstaff Hill Maritime Village tells the story of the Shipwreck Coast, and the beaches and river walks are right on the doorstep.

torquay.intro: Torquay is where the Great Ocean Road begins and where Australian surf culture took off: Rip Curl and Quiksilver both started here, and world-famous Bells Beach is just down the road. Expect surf beaches, the Australian National Surfing Museum and plenty of places to fuel up before the drive west.

st-kilda.intro: St Kilda is Melbourne’s bayside playground: the palm-lined Esplanade, Luna Park’s famous face, the cake shops of Acland Street and long sunset walks on the pier, where a colony of little penguins lives in the breakwater. It’s busy, a little scruffy and full of places to eat and drink.

mornington.intro: Mornington is the Mornington Peninsula’s main-street town, with a weekly Wednesday street market, a historic pier and the sheltered swimming at Mothers Beach. It’s the easy gateway to the peninsula’s wineries, hot springs and back beaches further south.

halls-gap.intro: Halls Gap is the village at the heart of the Grampians (Gariwerd) National Park, ringed by sandstone ranges. It’s the base for the park’s best-known walks and lookouts: the Pinnacle, MacKenzie Falls, and Boroka and Reed lookouts. Kangaroos graze the town oval at dusk, and the Brambuk cultural centre tells the story of the Jardwadjali and Djab Wurrung peoples.

dunkeld.intro: Dunkeld is a small town at the southern tip of the Grampians, under the peaks of Mount Sturgeon and Mount Abrupt. It punches far above its size for food, and the climb up Mount Sturgeon rewards you with views back across the range. It’s an easy stop between the Grampians and the coast.

port-fairy.intro: Port Fairy is a historic fishing village of whalers’ cottages, stone churches and a working harbour on the Moyne River. Walk out to the lighthouse on Griffiths Island, home to a shearwater colony, and time a visit for the Port Fairy Folk Festival in March if you like a crowd.

port-campbell.intro: Port Campbell is the small coastal town closest to the Twelve Apostles. Loch Ard Gorge, the Arch and London Bridge are all a short drive away along the Port Campbell National Park coastline. Stay the night so you can see the limestone stacks at sunset and again at sunrise, without the daytime crowds.

apollo-bay.intro: Apollo Bay is a fishing town where the Great Ocean Road meets the Otway Ranges. Head inland for rainforest walks and waterfalls in the Great Otway National Park, drive out to the Cape Otway Lightstation, or climb to Mariners Lookout for the view back over the bay.

lorne.intro: Lorne is the classic Great Ocean Road beach town, where the forest of the Otways comes right down to the sand. Swim or surf the main beach, walk out on the pier, then drive up to Teddy’s Lookout for the famous view of the road snaking along the coast, or into the hills to Erskine Falls.

wangaratta.intro: Wangaratta sits where the Ovens and King rivers meet, at the start of the Great Alpine Road. It’s the gateway to the King Valley’s Italian-heritage wineries and home to a well-known jazz and blues festival in spring.

myrtleford.intro: Myrtleford is a relaxed Ovens Valley town on the Great Alpine Road and the Murray to Mountains Rail Trail, with tobacco-kiln heritage, walnut and hop country around it, and Mount Buffalo looming to the south.

harrietville.intro: Harrietville is a tiny old gold-mining village at the foot of Mount Hotham, the last stop before the Great Alpine Road climbs into the mountains. It’s the start of the Razorback and Mount Feathertop walks for keen hikers.

mount-hotham.intro: Mount Hotham is one of Victoria’s highest alpine resorts, right on the Great Alpine Road. In winter it’s a ski and snowboard village; in summer the high plains open up for walking, wildflowers and huge views across the Alps. Carry chains in winter, as alpine road rules apply.

omeo.intro: Omeo is a remote high-country town on the Great Alpine Road between Hotham and Gippsland, with gold-rush history, a historic courthouse precinct and the Oriental Claims walk through old sluicing sites.

bairnsdale.intro: Bairnsdale is East Gippsland’s main town, where the Great Alpine Road meets the Princes Highway. It’s known for the painted ceiling of St Mary’s Church and makes an easy base for the Gippsland Lakes.

lakes-entrance.intro: Lakes Entrance is a seaside fishing town where the Gippsland Lakes meet Bass Strait. Walk the footbridge to Ninety Mile Beach, eat fish and chips off the trawlers and take a cruise on the lakes.

metung.intro: Metung is a small, pretty village on the shores of the Gippsland Lakes, made for boating, waterfront lunches and doing very little. It’s a short drive from Lakes Entrance and Bairnsdale.

sorrento.intro: Sorrento sits near the tip of the Mornington Peninsula, with calm bay beaches on one side and wild ocean back beaches on the other. Swim with the dolphins in summer, catch the ferry across to Queenscliff, or walk the coastal tracks of Point Nepean.

red-hill.intro: Red Hill is the peninsula’s wine and food heartland: rolling hills of cool-climate vineyards, cellar doors, orchards and a monthly community market. It’s the place for a long lunch.

dromana.intro: Dromana is a bayside town at the foot of Arthurs Seat. Ride the Eagle chairlift to the summit for views across Port Phillip Bay, then cool off at the beach.

flinders.intro: Flinders is a quiet village on Western Port with a historic pier, golf on the clifftops and some of the best rock-pool walks on the peninsula at Mushroom Reef.

healesville.intro: Healesville is the Yarra Valley’s main town, home to Healesville Sanctuary’s native wildlife and surrounded by wineries, a distillery and a chocolate factory. It’s an easy base for a valley day out.

yarra-glen.intro: Yarra Glen sits in the middle of the Yarra Valley wine country, close to some of the region’s best-known cellar doors, with hot-air balloon flights over the vineyards at dawn.

pages.title: About Vic Tours
pages.description: Vic Tours is a town-by-town guide to Victoria, made in Melbourne.
paragraphs: Vic Tours is a town-by-town guide to Victoria: where to stay, where to eat and what to do, in one place for each town and Melbourne neighbourhood.
It’s made in Melbourne by Independent Media Network Pty Ltd. We start with open data, so every listing is a real place, and add local knowledge on top.
Spotted something wrong or missing? Most listings come from OpenStreetMap, which anyone can improve, and fixes there flow back into our guides.

pages.title: How we build our guides
pages.description: Where Vic Tours’ listings come from, how we order them and how to correct them.
paragraphs: Listings come from OpenStreetMap, the free, community-edited map of the world (© OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database Licence).
Places with more complete details (website, opening hours, address) are shown first, and chain restaurants are listed last. We don’t accept payment for placement.
Distances are measured in a straight line from Melbourne’s CBD, so the drive is longer. Opening hours change, so check with the venue before you go.
Some links may become booking links in future. If they do, we’ll say so clearly on the page.

loops.name: Western Victoria Loop
loops.summary: Seven days from Melbourne: the goldfields, the Grampians and the Great Ocean Road, home along the coast.
loops.intro: A week-long self-drive loop through three of Victoria’s best regions. You head out through the gold-rush city of Ballarat, spend two nights among the Grampians’ ranges and waterfalls, then drop south to the Shipwreck Coast and drive the Great Ocean Road back towards Melbourne. Each day is a comfortable drive with plenty of time for walks, long lunches and lookouts.

days.title: Melbourne to Ballarat
days.text: An easy drive west to Ballarat. Spend the afternoon at Sovereign Hill or wander Lydiard and Sturt streets, then walk around Lake Wendouree as the sun goes down.

days.title: Ballarat to the Grampians
days.text: Head west into the Grampians. Settle into Halls Gap, then catch the late light from Boroka or Reed Lookout, and look for kangaroos on the town oval at dusk.

days.title: A day in the Grampians
days.text: Walk to the Pinnacle in the morning, then visit MacKenzie Falls in the afternoon. Brambuk is worth an hour for the region’s Aboriginal history and culture.

days.title: The Grampians to Port Fairy
days.text: Drive south through the range to Dunkeld for lunch beneath Mount Sturgeon, then continue down to the coast and into Port Fairy. Walk the Griffiths Island loop to the lighthouse before dinner.

days.title: The Shipwreck Coast
days.text: Stop in Warrnambool (whale season runs roughly May to September), then follow the coast east past the Bay of Islands to Port Campbell. Be at the Twelve Apostles or Loch Ard Gorge for sunset.

days.title: Through the Otways
days.text: Catch the Apostles at sunrise, then wind through the Otways to Apollo Bay for lunch, with a detour to Cape Otway or a rainforest waterfall. Finish the day on the beach at Lorne.

days.title: Lorne to Melbourne
days.text: Drive the most famous stretch of the Great Ocean Road, stopping at Teddy’s Lookout and the Memorial Arch, then surf-town Torquay and Bells Beach on the way back to Melbourne.

loops.name: Great Ocean Road in 3 days
loops.summary: The classic coastal drive from Torquay to the Twelve Apostles and Port Fairy, with two nights on the road.
loops.intro: Three days is the sweet spot for the Great Ocean Road: enough time to stop at the lookouts, walk into the Otways and see the Twelve Apostles at sunset, without rushing. You drive west along the coast and come home on the faster inland highway.

days.title: Melbourne to Lorne
days.text: Start in Torquay for a coffee and a look at Bells Beach, then pass under the Memorial Arch onto the coast road proper. Stop at Split Point Lighthouse at Aireys Inlet, then roll into Lorne for a swim and Teddy’s Lookout at the end of the day.

days.title: Lorne to the Twelve Apostles
days.text: The most dramatic stretch of the road. Lunch in Apollo Bay, then head into the Otways for a rainforest walk or out to Cape Otway. Keep driving to Port Campbell and be at the Twelve Apostles or Loch Ard Gorge for sunset.

days.title: Port Campbell to Port Fairy and home
days.text: See the Apostles again at sunrise without the crowds, then follow the coast past London Bridge and the Bay of Islands to Warrnambool. Finish in Port Fairy with a walk around Griffiths Island before taking the inland highway back to Melbourne (about 3.5 hours).

loops.name: Phillip Island day trip
loops.summary: Pelicans, seals, koalas and the Penguin Parade at dusk, in one big day from Melbourne.
loops.intro: Phillip Island is about two hours from Melbourne, and the best day there ends at dusk with the Penguin Parade. Plan the day backwards from that: arrive late morning, take it slow, and book your penguin viewing ahead in busy seasons.

days.title: Melbourne to Phillip Island and back
days.text: Cross the bridge at San Remo, where pelicans gather at the jetty around midday. Spend the afternoon at the Nobbies boardwalk looking out to Seal Rocks, the Koala Conservation Reserve or Churchill Island’s heritage farm, with a late lunch in Cowes. Then head to Summerland Beach for the Penguin Parade as the little penguins come ashore at sunset, and drive home after dark.

loops.name: The Great Alpine Road
loops.summary: Wangaratta to the Gippsland Lakes over the top of Mount Hotham, one of Australia’s highest sealed roads.
loops.intro: The Great Alpine Road runs over 300 km from Wangaratta to Bairnsdale, climbing through the Ovens Valley and over Mount Hotham before dropping through the high country to the Gippsland Lakes. Allow four days with time for walks and long lunches. In winter, carry snow chains between Harrietville and Omeo, as alpine road rules apply.

days.title: Melbourne to Bright
days.text: Head up the Hume to Wangaratta, then turn onto the Great Alpine Road through the Ovens Valley. Stop in Myrtleford, and arrive in Bright in time for a walk along the river.

days.title: A day around Bright
days.text: Hire a bike for the rail trail, drive up Mount Buffalo for the gorge lookouts, or work your way through the valley’s breweries and wineries.

days.title: Over the mountain to Omeo
days.text: The big day. Climb from Harrietville over Mount Hotham, stopping at the lookouts along the way (check road conditions in winter), then wind down through the high plains to Omeo.

days.title: Omeo to the Gippsland Lakes
days.text: Follow the Tambo Valley down to Bairnsdale, then lunch on the water at Metung and finish at Lakes Entrance for fish and chips and a sunset walk on Ninety Mile Beach. Melbourne is about 4 hours home the next day.

loops.name: Mornington Peninsula day trip
loops.summary: Bay beaches, a chairlift ride, a winery lunch and the wild back beaches, about an hour from Melbourne.
loops.intro: The Mornington Peninsula packs bay beaches, wine country and wild ocean coastline into one easy loop from Melbourne. Drive down the bay side, cross the hills for lunch, and come home via Western Port.

days.title: A loop around the peninsula
days.text: Coffee and a wander on Mornington’s Main Street, then ride the Eagle at Arthurs Seat above Dromana. Lunch at a Red Hill cellar door, then head to Sorrento for the bay and a walk at the back beach. Come home via Flinders for the pier and Mushroom Reef rock pools at low tide.

loops.name: Yarra Valley day trip
loops.summary: Native wildlife, cellar doors and a long lunch, about an hour from Melbourne.
loops.intro: The Yarra Valley is Melbourne’s closest wine region, and it’s easy to fill a day with wildlife, wineries and food. If you’re tasting, book a driver or tour.

days.title: Healesville and the valley
days.text: Start early at Healesville Sanctuary for koalas, platypus and the birds of prey show. Then work your way through the valley’s cellar doors around Yarra Glen for a long winery lunch, with a chocolate or cheese stop on the way home.
